extracted.intended_audience: aspiring satirical writers, journalism students, and readers interested in media history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for producing American-style news satire (Onion-style): headline-driven parody using journalistic voice, editorial pitching, ethical boundaries, and format/multimedia strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize current news and parody hard-news headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Onion satirizes current news and makes a parody of USA Today and hard news style headlines.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the conventions and look of straight news headlines to lampoon actual current events. Examples from the piece include: “Trump’s Support Surges After He Points Gun at Nation,” “Man Who Bumped Tesla While Parallel Parking Sentenced To Death,” and “Teen Warned Not To Accept Group Chat Invites From National Security Advisors She Doesn’t Know.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Use news rhetoric and a neutral journalistic voice to reveal absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: “They try to use news rhetoric and journalistic conventions to reveal the absurdity of politics... ‘You have people doing completely ludicrous and insane things, and you’re trying to talk about them in this neutral news voice, and it just comes off like insanity, right?’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the factual tone and structure of journalism (neutral voice, inverted pyramid feel, dateline-style phrasing) so that the juxtaposition of style and content highlights the absurdity. Be aware that when real life is already extreme, the technique can sometimes fail or read as reality instead of satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensive pitch meetings with high idea-volume and strict selection
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Onion is well known for its intensive pitch meetings, where out of every 100 headline ideas, about two or three get selected.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize quantity and rapid idea generation in group editorial sessions; rely on rigorous selection to keep only the strongest material. The piece also notes The Onion aimed to publish only the best five to ten percent of ideas, crediting this editorial discipline for longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish and maintain a signature voice
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the website went up in 1996, The Onion had established its signature voice, and was the first fully formed humor website on the internet…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a consistent, recognizable tone that carries across pieces and platforms. Early clarity of voice helped The Onion explode online and attract a worldwide audience; maintaining that voice supports brand identity even as formats change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch up rather than punch down
rubrics_metrics.description: “Both Wenc and Nackers emphasized The Onion’s efforts to navigate political satire by punching up, rather than punching down...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target power structures, institutions, and those with greater power rather than marginalized groups. The Onion generally took a progressive stance and sought to critique both Democrats and Republicans, but must monitor when material crosses the line into punching down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt to reacting to news rather than predicting it in a volatile landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: “With a shifting political landscape in the U.S., especially in regard to Trump’s election and presidency, The Onion has adapted to reacting to rather than predicting news.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize timely responses to current events rather than attempting to forecast them; stay agile editorially to address rapidly changing political climates. This shift was driven by changes in the news environment and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not beholden to mainstream media; act as truth-tellers using satire
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’re not beholden to anybody like the mainstream media reporters are,” Nackers said. “So, we can kind of be the truth tellers and do that in a funny way.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relative freedom of satirical outlets to critique conventional journalism and power with fewer institutional constraints; leverage satire to reveal truths that straight reporting may avoid or soften.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect audience cultural sensibilities and align tone to readership
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wisconsinites generally have a naturally self-aware and dry sense of humor, which The Onion captured perfectly...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the tastes, cultural norms, and expectations of your primary audience when shaping tone and targets. A receptive audience and cultural fit can amplify reach and resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge ethical boundaries and be prepared to correct or learn from missteps
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that while The Onion emphasizes punching up, “both acknowledged that some content has crossed that line.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain internal standards and be willing to reassess pieces that may have inadvertently harmed or targeted vulnerable groups. Editorial rigor and willingness to confront past errors help sustain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify formats (online, multimedia, print) while preserving editorial standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onion’s early internet presence (website launch 1996) drove success; the organization later expanded into a production company, moved operations, and even brought back its print edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grow into multimedia and different distribution channels to reach wider audiences, but keep the core editorial process and selection standards consistent across formats so quality and voice remain intact.
